transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-08 UTC
Start: 15:30
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Connor (Redwood SE), Lara (NexisPay CTO), Diego (Platform), Priya (SRE), Samir (Product)

[00:00] Maya: All right, thanks everyone for joining. This is Maya from Redwood. Quick agenda — recap of last week's throughput numbers, tune autoscale thresholds, and confirm the dry-run spike next week. Connor will lead the technical detail.
[00:18] Lara: Yep, thanks. We only have about 45 minutes, so want to cover the key pain points — we saw a tail latency spike in last Friday's test and want to avoid user impact.
[00:28] Connor: Uh-huh, yeah. So the spike — I looked at the run and the main issue was that when the request queue hit the 95th percentile, the Dedicated pool didn't scale until after a 90s cooldown which let latency climb. We suggested lowering the cool down and adding a small reserved headroom buffer.
[00:45] Diego: Can you define reserved headroom again? Is that the extra instances we keep idle?
[00:52] Connor: Kind of — it's a configuration where reserved capacity is pinned for sudden bursts; effectively you keep X GPUs pre-provisioned or reserved so warm-up time is zero for that level. It's cheaper than overprovisioning if bursts are short.
[01:10] Priya: Question — how does pre-warm interact with the KV cache and cold-starting the model? We saw token-generation delay even when containers came up.
[01:22] Connor: Good point. The runtime has two stages: container warm, and KV cache / model weights warmed. For large models the KV cache filling and quantization paths can add 3-10s of extra per-instance warm time. Pre-warm does container + partial KV warm for a set of common prefixes; full KV fill is progressive as traffic hits. That explains the residual latency.
[01:45] Samir: So what's the recommended policy? Lower cooldown from 90 to 30? Keep a reserved buffer of 10%?
[01:52] Connor: For your traffic profile — which is bursty but short (you said under an hour) — I'd suggest: target 30s cooldown, step-scaling by 1-2 GPUs at 75th/85th percentiles, and a reserved headroom of 8-12% capacity. Also pre-warm one extra instance for the initial spike window.
[02:18] Lara: Are those numbers modeled against our 95th percentile throughput? I need to justify to finance.
[02:25] Maya: We ran a cost sim — Connor, you had a quick chart?
[02:28] Connor: Yeah I posted a simple sim in the shared doc: with 10% headroom the marginal monthly cost was about a 6% increase but it reduced the spike latency by roughly 60% in our tests. Note that if you use quantized variants the cost delta is smaller but quality differences need checking.
[02:52] Diego: Quick call out — Samir mentioned fallback to hosted variant if Dedicated capacity is exhausted. How seamless is that, and does it impact data residency?
[03:03] Maya: Good question. Fallback routing is policy-driven. You can mark certain routes to failover to a hosted model variant in another region; that does cross boundaries, so if you have strict data residency requirements we can instead route to a Dedicated standby in a compliant region or queue requests. We documented the options in the playbook.
[03:28] Priya: And logs — will we still get token-level traces when routing to hosted? We need the observability to debug.
[03:34] Connor: Yes, the tracing hooks persist; telemetry will say 'served-by: hosted-variant' and we keep a flag in logs. Some PII redaction and KMS wrapping policies may vary, so we'll surface that in the security notes.
[03:50] Lara: Can we talk about surge shaping? We want to smooth spikes at the edge rather than rely completely on backend scaling.
[03:58] Diego: We can do a small queue + token-throttling at the gateway. But we worry about user retry storms if latency increases.
[04:05] Connor: The recommended approach is two layers: 1) edge shaping with a short queue and leaky-bucket smoothing to absorb microbursts; 2) backend reserved headroom plus fast step-scaling. That combo reduced dropped requests in our sim.
[04:22] Samir: Practical question — what's the timeline for the dry-run? We want to align with our SRE on-call rotation.
[04:28] Maya: Proposed next Wednesday 04/15 for a 1-hour window. Diego, can you confirm the traffic shape and SR rotation?
[04:33] Diego: I'll confirm by Monday. I'll also send the CSV of the traffic shape.
[04:37] Priya: For the dry-run we'll need the Private deployment checklist and the KMS integration doc — I have a few compliance questions.
[04:44] Maya: We'll send the Private checklist and KMS notes by Friday. Connor, you'll add the runbook snippet for pre-warm and fallback?
[04:49] Connor: Yup, I'll have a runbook snippet and example autoscale YAML with comments.
[05:00] Lara: Another issue — last test showed some CPU bursts in the routing layer even when GPU pool scaled. Any ideas?
[05:06] Connor: That was likely due to request deserialization and response post-processing. We recommended moving heavy transforms into batch jobs or running a small pool of async workers. Also ensure instrumentation on the routing layer — we're shipping a small tracer that tags request size and processing time.
[05:26] Diego: Can you also add an example of cooldown per-route? Some of our routes are very latency-sensitive and others are background.
[05:33] Connor: Absolutely — you can define per-route SLOs and scale policies. We'll include defaults: latency-sensitive route has lower scale thresholds and less aggressive cooldown.
[05:43] Samir: About quantized models — we tested a 4-bit variant and saw slightly lower quality on some prompts. Do you recommend fallback logic to a higher precision model for those cases?
[05:54] Connor: Yes, you can do model-variant routing: try quantized by default, if generation score/confidence drops below a threshold, escalate to a higher precision variant (or route to hosted). It's a trade-off between cost and quality. We'll show an eval harness example.
[06:12] Lara: Okay, let's summarize next steps and owners.
[06:16] Maya: I'll share the autoscale YAML and telemetry charts by Saturday. Connor will prepare runbook & pre-warm snippet by Monday. Diego will send traffic CSV by Monday. Priya will route compliance questions and KMS contacts by Friday. We'll schedule the dry-run for next Wednesday 04/15.
[06:33] Priya: One last quick item - do you have an estimate of S L A impact if we do fallback to hosted? Finance asked about potential contractual impact.
[06:40] Maya: Fallback to hosted doesn't change your Dedicated SLA; it just introduces a potential difference in latency and the hosted SLA applies to that path. We can draft language for your procurement team.
[06:52] Lara: Great. Anything else?
[06:55] Samir: No, thanks everyone.
[06:58] Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the doc links.

Notes on transcription: some terms transcribed roughly (K V cache -> KV cache, S L A -> SLA), occasional overlaps. Shared links: doc://redwood/nexispay/autoscale-sim (referenced), doc://redwood/policies/fallback-playbook.
